probe: ticket 0025 X2, mechanism annex — where the 4,5x on p95 comes from, and what it buys in results. Same index and same two arms as x2-verdict.json.
method: Each query's term set is rebuilt exactly as each arm's tokenize() produces it (fold, split on non-alphanumerics, drop 1-char tokens, drop the stoplist on the control only, dedupe as sqlite-index.ts:466 does), then every term is looked up in the fts5vocab table of the measured index. No cost model and no fitted constant: the posting counts are the work FTS5 has to do, and they sit beside the measured time.

corpus.note: The 29 stoplist words are 29 of 639 888 distinct terms — 0,005% of the vocabulary — and 21,8% of all token occurrences. That concentration is the whole phenomenon: a rounding error in the dictionary, a fifth of the corpus.

sublinearity: Work rises 37,0x and time only 5,6x, so FTS5 walks a long posting list far more cheaply per entry than a short one (1 063,8 ns -> 159,6 ns). The engine is not behaving badly; it is being asked to do 37 times more work and doing it efficiently. That is why the deletion is a design problem rather than a bug to optimise away.

what_it_buys.reading: 88% of the top-20 is unchanged, 19 of 20 queries keep the same first hit, and 11 of 20 return an identical list. The PR's own justification explains this and cuts against it: bm25 already down-weights ubiquitous terms, so adding them buys almost no ranking while costing 5,6x the time. The single query whose results genuinely change is `to be or not to be` (25% overlap) — the degenerate case, which is where the whole value sits.

collateral_costs_not_in_the_pr.memory_backend_index_growth: bm25.ts addDoc() runs tokenize() over the DOCUMENT too, so on the memory backend the deletion is symmetric and the in-memory postings grow by the stopword share: 21,8% more tokens, tf entries and df entries. Not measured here (X2 ran on sqlite), and material for a project whose uncapped build already peaks near 1,8 GiB.
collateral_costs_not_in_the_pr.snippet_regression: makeSnippet() centres the excerpt on the EARLIEST position of any query token. `the` occurs near the start of almost every passage, so with the stoplist gone the excerpt collapses onto the passage opening instead of the matched content. Demonstrated on a synthetic passage: stock returns the sentence containing 'elasticity of substitution'; the deleted arm returns the paper's boilerplate first sentence.

lexical_semantic_interaction.fusion: index-manager.ts:1131 — rrf([keyword, vector]), Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60 over a pool of 3x the requested limit. Rank-based, so bm25 scores never reach the fusion; only the ORDER of the keyword list matters.
lexical_semantic_interaction.consequence_for_x2: Because RRF reads order and the order is 88% preserved, the fused result moves even less than the lexical result does. The deletion buys less in hybrid mode than in keyword mode, at the same cost.
lexical_semantic_interaction.stoplist_touches_only_the_lexical_path: The semantic path embeds the raw query string (`embedder.embed([q])`); tokenize() is never applied to it. So the stoplist has no effect on semantic retrieval either way.
lexical_semantic_interaction.the_two_run_in_sequence: keywordSearch() is synchronous and completes before `await embedder.embed(...)` begins, so in the default `auto` mode the keyword latency ADDS to the embed-plus-vector latency. X2 measured mode:'keyword' with embeddings off, which is correct for isolating the deletion — but it means 1 773,0 ms is a FLOOR for what a default-mode user would wait, not a ceiling.
lexical_semantic_interaction.the_degenerate_case_is_already_covered: A query made only of function words is exactly the case the semantic path handles well: it embeds the whole string, function words included. So in `auto` mode with an embedder configured, the failure the deletion exists to fix is largely already handled. REASONED FROM THE CODE, NOT MEASURED — X2 ran with embeddings off. Worth one measurement before anyone leans on it.

cheaper_alternative_worth_weighing: Keep the stoplist and fall back to the unfiltered token set when filtering leaves too few terms. Normal queries pay nothing — the 88%-identical results stay identical at 392,3 ms — and the degenerate query is fixed, paying its ~900 ms only when it occurs. df-driven pruning, which DESIGN §3 names, solves a problem this repo has now measured as mostly not worth solving: it would spend real complexity to make a 5,6x regression smaller, where the fallback avoids incurring it. Both are language- neutral. The fallback is also a far smaller diff to ask an upstream maintainer to take.
